source.title: Detoxify Language Model Step-by-Step
source.authors: Zecheng Tang; Ke-Yan Zhou; Pinzheng Wang; Yu-Yang Ding; Jun-Tao Li; Min Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, with flattened tables and an appended response-to-reviewers document.
record.tranche_reason: Compares detoxification-task outcomes for two LLaMA 2 parameter sizes after CMD training. It does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute; small-run extrapolation; compute-optimal allocations; or architecture-controlled loss comparisons. Its parameter-size comparison reports detoxification outcomes for CMD-trained LLaMA 2 models, bearing on V6. Other detoxification comparisons and cited results do not test the scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: This is a detoxification-method paper. Its only size comparison is two LLaMA 2 sizes (7B, 13B) after the authors' own CMD LoRA fine-tuning, scored for toxicity. That is a measure of their method's effect, not a test of whether task performance scales predictably with model size or pretraining loss. It reports no pretraining loss, no fitted scaling relation and no extrapolation. The authors' remark about toxicity versus model size is a passing observation from two points, so the study neither tests nor uses the scaling-law versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct for the size remark, which is a side observation. The paper's main conclusion is that CMD, which detoxifies the context and then generates along it with a toxic contrastive loss, achieves the best balance of detoxification and generation quality compared with baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates detoxification outcomes after CMD LoRA fine-tuning; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law loss measurements or compute-allocation experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Generation toxicity on RealToxicityPrompts is nearly identical for LLaMA2-7B and 13B, both before CMD (Exp. Max. Toxicity 0.40 vs 0.40; Toxicity Prob. 29.80% vs 30.70%) and after CMD (4.30% vs 4.90%). The authors attribute toxicity to training data rather than model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompted toxic generation rate does not change with model size within a model family (7B to 13B).

record.problems: The parameter-size comparison covers only two LLaMA 2 sizes and one CMD fine-tuning setup. It reports detoxification metrics, not held-out pretraining loss or a fitted scaling relationship; no statistical test details for the stated lack of significant differences are provided in the text.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from fitted small runs.
All: no shape-versus-loss comparison at fixed parameter count.
All: no power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
No downstream capability measured across a scale series, and no link to pretraining loss.
All: no fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' classification and its V6 'challenges' label are rejected. Toxicity of a detox-fine-tuned model at two sizes is a property of the method, not a scaling-law measure. The stated lack of significant difference comes with no statistical test.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations across compute budgets.
Controlled comparisons of architecture details at fixed parameter count and their effect on loss.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance relationships, other downstream tasks, and a broader range of model sizes.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.
